A live test of how blue-state shield statutes will hold up if SCOTUS lets the appellate ruling stand — reverberating in NY, MA, NJ, and CO, all watching CT’s next legislative move.

title: Texas lawmakers back lifting camp safety rule made after flood
why: Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and Speaker Dustin Burrows publicly asked the state health agency to lift the fiber-optics requirement adopted after the 2025 Camp Mystic disaster, after camps complained the rule is unworkable. The first concrete step backward in the Camp Mystic regulatory tug-of-war — directly relevant to the parallel youth-camp regulation drafts now underway in Tennessee, North Carolina, and Connecticut.

title: Tennessee legislature redistricting session: What to expect
why: Detailed preview of Gov. Lee’s called special session: most of the state’s nine congressional districts will be redrawn, with the explicit goal of cracking the Memphis-anchored 9th — the state’s only Democrat-controlled and only majority-Black district. The clearest mid-decade gerrymandering escalation since Texas; Virginia, Missouri, and Indiana are watching how fast Tennessee can move it through and what legal pushback materializes.

title: Group tied to Democratic leadership in US House is funding attempt to redraw Colorado’s congressional map
why: A nonprofit tied to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is financing a Colorado redistricting effort that would shift the state’s congressional delegation from 4D-4R to a Democratic-favored 7D-1R. The first openly funded Democratic counter-gerrymander aimed at offsetting Texas and Tennessee’s GOP redraws — escalating the nationwide arms race documented elsewhere in this run.

title: Jefferson County judge’s ruling challenges constitutionality of unlawful camping ban
why: A Jefferson County District Court judge ruled Monday that Kentucky’s camping ban targeting people experiencing homelessness is unconstitutional — a direct counter to the Supreme Court’s Grants Pass v. Johnson decision that greenlit similar bans nationally. The first state-court ruling of its kind in a Republican-led state and a precedent that homelessness advocates in Tennessee, Florida, and Texas will lean on to challenge their own statutes.

title: Cook County Landlords Have Filed For More Than 40,000 Evictions Since 2022
why: Block Club’s 4-year filings analysis surfaces a 45-year-old South Shore tenant whose new owner raised her rent 60% in a month before suing to evict; the dataset behind her case maps the broader displacement pattern in 40,000+ Cook County eviction filings since 2022. Pairs directly with last week’s ICE-tied “Brink of Eviction” report — a reproducible eviction-data methodology Detroit, Houston, and LA are already starting to clone.

title: CT adopts homeschool regulation over staunch objection from GOP
why: Connecticut's Senate gave 22-14 final passage just before midnight Monday to the state's first-ever homeschool registration and reporting regime — a measure unsuccessfully fought as government overreach for the entirety of session. The first regulatory framework on homeschooling adopted in nearly a decade nationally; Maine, Massachusetts, and New Jersey lawmakers had been waiting on this outcome before moving their own drafts.

title: General Assembly passes bill to regulate earmarks amid probe
why: CT Senate gave final passage Monday to a transparency bill responding directly to a political scandal involving discretionary legislative earmarks — disclosure rules and procedural guardrails the legislature is putting on itself. The kind of mid-scandal accountability fix other state legislatures (NY, MA, IL) facing parallel earmark transparency fights now have a working template for.

title: Box Elder County OKs massive data center project backed by celebrity investor
why: After last week's delay and hundreds of protesters, the three-member Box Elder County Commission gave final approval Monday to MIDA's 40,000-acre Stratos hyperscale data center backed by Kevin O'Leary, despite the deluge of state-agency comments about Great Salt Lake water and grid impacts. Closes the Utah chapter of the same data-center-vs-community fight playing out almost identically in WI (Port Washington), AZ (Tucson), and TX (Fort Bliss) — a green light other state-vs-county authorities will now confront.

title: Louisiana Lawmakers Move to Eliminate Office Won by Black Candidate
why: Calvin Duncan — who won 68% of the vote to become Orleans Parish Criminal District Court clerk — reported to work Monday after a federal judge enjoined a Republican-passed law abolishing the office, only to be blocked hours later when the Fifth Circuit paused that ruling pending the Louisiana Supreme Court. A clean voting-rights and federal-state-court chess case other Southern outlets covering Black candidate suppression (GA, MS, AL) will track closely.

title: Civil rights groups sue to stop Texas immigration law
why: A coalition of civil rights organizations filed a fresh lawsuit Monday to block parts of Senate Bill 4 — the law that would let Texas police arrest people suspected of crossing the U.S.-Mexico border illegally — just days before it can take effect after a Fifth Circuit panel lifted the years-long injunction. The result is the most consequential live state-immigration-enforcement case in the country, and a direct preview of how the same kind of state arrest authority pursued in Florida, Tennessee, and Iowa fares against constitutional preemption challenges.

title: ICE Raids Have Chicago's Immigrant Tenants On 'Brink Of Eviction,' Report Finds
why: New report quantifies the cascade from ICE arrests to lost wages to back rent: families thousands of dollars behind, with advocates urging City Council to enact a blanket eviction moratorium. The first hard data on the housing-loss spillover of urban immigration enforcement — a frame Detroit, Houston, and LA outlets are now testing against their own jurisdictions' eviction filings.

title: Trump's immigration crackdown in Colorado, explained in 3 charts
why: Federal data-driven explainer documenting that ICE arrests in Colorado tripled to ~12 per day in 2025 from four in 2024, with charts breaking out arrest type, country of origin, and detention transfer. A reproducible methodology other state-focused outlets in CT, MN, and OH can clone to benchmark enforcement intensity in their own jurisdictions.

title: Nearly 96,000 students receiving Texas school voucher award notices
why: Acting Comptroller Kelly Hancock said in a Monday statement that ~96,000 students will receive Education Savings Account award notices by May 6 — the rollout of the largest state-funded school-choice program in U.S. history. The participation numbers, school-type breakdowns, and award sizes set the empirical baseline every state pursuing similar voucher programs (Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia) will use as their argument template.

title: Will San Diego County vote on a half-cent sales tax this year? What to know
why: Proposed county half-cent sales tax could generate $367M annually — carved between healthcare, public safety, and a chunk earmarked for fixes to the cross-border Tijuana River pollution crisis. The mechanism (one tax, three priorities, including a binational environmental disaster) is the only working blueprint other border counties (El Paso, Pima, Imperial) have to fund their own untreated-flow problems.

title: Video Appears to Show ICE Agent Tasing Man Multiple Times Ahead of Bushwick Hospital Standoff
why: THE CITY obtained video that appears to show an ICE agent tasing a man repeatedly while another agent tries to drag him from his car ahead of a standoff at Wyckoff Heights hospital. Mayor Mamdani used the footage to publicly reaffirm NYPD will not assist civil immigration enforcement — the most concrete operational test yet of his sanctuary-policy posture and a model other big-city mayors are watching as ICE escalates urban enforcement.

title: Check layoff numbers for your California school district
why: More than 2,400 preliminary teacher layoff notices and 3,300 classified-staff notices have hit California districts ahead of the May 15 finalization deadline — an interactive tool lets readers check totals district-by-district. A bellwether for how the most populous blue state is absorbing the same federal Title I, IDEA, and ESSER cliff that's already squeezing districts in Texas, Colorado, and Washington.

title: CT legislature adopts $28B budget with big aid for towns, childcare
why: Connecticut adopted a $28.1B two-year budget Saturday that restructures the hospital tax to leverage more federal Medicaid dollars, fully funds free breakfast at every public school, and channels new money into municipal aid and affordable childcare. The hospital-tax restructuring in particular is the kind of federal-leverage maneuver other Medicaid-expansion states (CO, VT, NY) are quietly studying as Washington squeezes the program.

title: Wisconsin will likely see limited, local effects from Voting Rights Act ruling — at least for now
why: First detailed state-level read on how the Supreme Court's Louisiana v. Callais decision actually plays out: Wisconsin's congressional and legislative maps mostly survive, but Milwaukee city council and school district boundaries drawn explicitly along racial lines are now exposed to challenges. A reproducible analytical template every other northern state will lean on as local-jurisdiction VRA suits land in the next budget cycle.

title: Sweeping labor legislation poised for final passage in CT Senate
why: H.B. 5003 makes general contractors liable for subcontractors' wage theft with double damages, raises workers'-comp benefits to 100% of lost wages for assault victims in healthcare and schools, and protects service workers from termination for 90 days after a contract change-of-hands. The wage-theft provision in particular is exactly the model the NYC Comptroller-Parks playbook (covered in last week's THE CITY scoop) has been pushing — CT becoming the first state to codify it makes this a national template.

title: Lawmakers race to finish data privacy bill amid outcry from businesses and medical providers
why: S.71 would give Vermonters access, correction, and deletion rights over data held by covered entities, plus tight rules on collection of sensitive categories like medical info and ID numbers. Opposition from 100+ businesses and the Vermont Medical Society (which says the bill duplicates HIPAA) is the same coalition that has flattened similar bills in Maine, Massachusetts, and Maryland — Vermont's outcome is a real test of whether the state-by-state privacy patchwork can survive professional-association pushback.

title: Colorado's AI compromise would focus regulations on informing consumers when the technology is used
why: Senate Bill 189 would push Colorado's first-in-the-nation AI antidiscrimination law back to January 2027 and gut its disclosure-and-impact-assessment regime in favor of a notice-only approach. The retreat lands while DOJ and Elon Musk's xAI are actively suing the original law in federal court — a major rollback that every other state legislature drafting AI rules (CA, TX, NY) is now using as the new ceiling for what's politically defensible.

title: Investigation of Supreme Court justice should be independent, Utah Gov. Cox says — not a 'witch hunt'
why: Cox said publicly Friday that the governor has no constitutional role in the disciplinary investigation of Utah Supreme Court Justice Diana Hagen — a notable distancing move after the state high court itself ruled the existing investigation was illegally released. A clean separation-of-powers signal in a moment when other Republican governors (FL, TX, MO) are explicitly testing how far executives can lean on judicial-discipline processes.

title: 'Death By a Thousand Cuts': Longer Renewal Times Are Making DACA Recipients Deportable
why: Documented reconstructs how stretched USCIS processing times — paired with a new Board of Immigration Appeals precedent that ends DACA's automatic shield against removal — are turning routine renewals into deportation triggers for some of the 505,940 active DACA recipients nationwide, including 19,580 in New York. A measurable enforcement shift other immigration-focused outlets in El Paso, Houston, and Minnesota can immediately replicate against their own caseloads.

title: Bill Lee calls special session for Tennessee redistricting
why: Gov. Lee summoned the General Assembly to redraw Tennessee's congressional map after Trump and Sen. Marsha Blackburn pushed to crack the Memphis-based 9th, the state's only majority-Black district. The move escalates a nationwide mid-decade gerrymandering war that started in Texas — Virginia, Missouri, and Indiana are watching how fast Tennessee can move and what kind of legal pushback materializes.

title: Staff at Justice-Focused Nonprofits Launch Union Push
why: About 600 caseworkers, career coaches, and housing specialists at the Fortune Society and Osborne Association — two re-entry nonprofits with a combined $593M in active city contracts — kicked off a unionization drive on May Day, backed by Local 153 of OPEIU and a letter signed by more than a dozen Council members. A direct labor-organizing test for Mamdani's progressive base inside the very nonprofit sector that helped elect him.

title: Gov. Stein signs Medicaid funding bill despite concerns about some provisions
why: Stein signed House Bill 696 Thursday, releasing $319 million from the Medicaid Contingency Reserve to keep North Carolina's program solvent through June. Same pressure test — federal cost shifts, GLP-1 uptake, autism-treatment demand — every Medicaid-expansion state is about to face; CT, CO, and VT are watching how Stein navigates the provisions he flagged for follow-up.

title: Utah obligated to build 'hyperscale' data center backed by Kevin O'Leary, Cox says
why: Gov. Spencer Cox said Thursday the state believes it is contractually locked in to the $4 billion Box Elder hyperscale data center despite this week's commission delay and mounting water/grid pushback. The state-vs-county fight over hyperscale buildouts is now playing out almost identically in WI, AZ, and TX — Cox's framing accelerates a clash AI infrastructure pessimists across the country are watching.

title: Vermont lawmakers no longer plan on unmasking ICE
why: House Judiciary gutted S.208 after a federal appeals court last week ruled California's similar mask-ban law unconstitutional — the new version no longer applies to federal agents and stops short of banning state and local police from concealing identities. A direct preemption ripple every state legislature pursuing unmasking bills (NY, NJ, MA, CA) now has to recalibrate against.

title: Texas DACA recipient detained again after ICE deported him, then allowed his return
why: Jose Contreras Diaz was detained on arrival at Brownsville after ICE earlier deported him to Honduras and then conceded — in writing — that his DACA status entitled him to be in the country. The deportation→return→redetention pattern is starting to show up in border-outlet reporting (El Paso Matters, AZ Mirror) as a measurable enforcement shift, not just isolated incidents.

title: A major Vermont employer supplies helmets used by ICE
why: VTDigger matched distinctive design features of helmets worn by federal agents at high-profile ICE operations — including the daylong March standoff in South Burlington — to those made by Vermont-based Galvion. DHS signed a $15.5M contract for Galvion helmets starting September 2025, putting the state's largest defense employer squarely in the federal-immigration-enforcement procurement story other state outlets can now replicate.

title: No payout for fracking waste company that caused earthquakes, Ohio court says
why: Unanimous Ohio Supreme Court rejection of D&L Energy's takings claim ends 12 years of litigation tied to two Trumbull County earthquakes induced by injection wells — the regulator's right to suspend operations stands. A direct precedent oil-and-gas regulators in Oklahoma, Texas, and West Virginia will now lean on when industry pushes back on shutdown orders.

title: Texas' Camp Mystic won't reopen this summer
why: Camp Mystic withdrew its operating-license application Thursday — the formal closure that follows this week's Eastland family apology and the legislative committee hearings concluding counselors were untrained and the camp had no flood plan. The pivotal point in a national private-youth-camp regulation fight other states are now openly drafting bills around.

title: Forgery and Wage Theft: Playground Contractors Hit With Massive Fines
why: Joint Comptroller-Parks investigation into the Hunts Point Playground rebuild documents 24 workers paid below prevailing wage and forced into kickbacks, with forged affidavits used to cover the trail. Two firms debarred and ordered to pay $618,495.40 in restitution and penalties — a reproducible labor-enforcement playbook other muni comptrollers can copy.

title: With ban in doubt, Colorado considers new law targeting conversion therapy
why: House Bill 1322 reframes conversion therapy as harmful professional conduct rather than prohibited speech — a workaround designed to survive the Supreme Court's Chiles ruling on free-speech grounds. Civil suits with no statute of limitations and licensing-board exposure for mental-health providers; a model other states whose bans are now on shaky ground will study closely.

title: Leaving office, Erin Stewart sought pension benefit that didn't exist
why: Outgoing New Britain mayor and 2026 GOP gubernatorial frontrunner Erin Stewart asked the city for a partial pension benefit it doesn't actually offer — and pursued it as she eyes statewide office. A clean accountability scoop on a top-tier Connecticut candidate that ripples through every other open-seat governor's race watching how candidates handle their last municipal exit.

title: Texas Hispanic GOP candidates aim to keep the Latino vote red
why: Up to six Hispanic Republicans could be on the November ballot in Texas' most contested congressional races, with Webb County Judge Tano Tijerina headlining the slate against Cuellar. The piece tracks the GOP's coalitional bet that Trump's 2024 Latino gains can survive ICE raids on construction sites — a test the rest of the Sun Belt is watching closely.

title: CT Senate OKs four years of raises for unionized state employees
why: Senate ratified the new four-year SEBAC contract with raises that codify Lamont's already-pledged step increases, locking in personnel costs through the next governor's term. A direct read on how blue-state public-employee compensation is going to compound just as Medicaid cuts are squeezing budgets — and a fight other Northeastern legislatures are about to relive.

title: Vermont Senate advances property tax bill with a 3.8% average increase
why: Senators advanced H.949 using $100.9M in surplus to buy down property taxes — closer to Gov. Scott's plan than the House's, which would have stashed half the surplus. The Senate Finance amendment also expands the renter credit by $4M, a small but real concession in a state where property-tax pain has been the dominant kitchen-table issue going into the midterms.

title: Mayor Freddie O'Connell delivers 2026 State of Metro speech
why: O'Connell's FY27 budget, unveiled at Nissan Stadium, cuts the city grocery tax, launches a revolving affordable-housing loan program designed to seed a future bond, and adds a grant program for legacy local businesses — all while keeping the property tax rate flat. The grocery-tax cut paired with a housing fund makes Nashville a test case for blue-city affordability politics under a hostile state legislature.

title: New York Immigration Talks Hit Impasse After Hochul's Latest Proposal
why: Hochul's newest budget offer drops the probable-cause requirement for local-cop coordination with ICE in criminal cases — a reversal from her April 16 compromise. Legislators backing immigrant protections told NYF they'd rather walk than sign on, leaving the late state budget stalled into May with the immigration plank as the central sticking point.

title: Detroit crypto landlord RealT cedes portfolio control to third party
why: Outside fiduciary Charles Bullock takes over RealT's roughly 700 Detroit properties, with authority to renovate at the company's expense, sell to raise cash, and demolish what's beyond saving — a rare housing-accountability win as the city's nuisance suit advances. The agreement targets repairs at ≈12 properties per month, with 210 brought into compliance by October 2027.

title: Immigration News Today: Appeals Court Rules Against Trump Admin.'s Mandatory Detention Policy
why: A federal appeals court ruled the Trump administration cannot indefinitely detain noncitizens with longstanding U.S. ties without bond hearings, narrowing the September 2025 BIA decision that had vastly expanded mandatory detention. Documented walks through the immediate caseload impact for New York's immigration courts — and flags the circuit-split risk that puts the issue on a collision course with the Supreme Court.

title: Tennessee's public school funding drops to lowest in the U.S.
why: New NEA data has Tennessee dead last (51st) at $12,147 per pupil after a 9.8% one-year drop — the steepest single-year decline of any state. Lands as the legislature's voucher expansion goes statewide and gives every other Southern state pushing similar voucher programs (Alabama, Georgia, Florida) a benchmark to argue against.

title: Mamdani's 'Economic Justice' Deputy Wants a Bigger Pie
why: Profile of Deputy Mayor Julie Su, ex-Biden Labor official, outlining a memo that pushes EDC to evaluate tax breaks by job quality not just count — with union-labor strings attached. Sets the policy frame for how Mamdani's administration will fight Citadel and other big-employer threats, and gives every progressive mayor a model memo to copy.

title: What we know about the surprise CMS Board rejection of Superintendent Hill's budget
why: WFAE's morning explainer reconstructs the 8-1 Charlotte-Mecklenburg school board vote against Superintendent Crystal Hill's $2.1B budget — a rare unanimous-minus-one rebuke of a superintendent the same board members publicly praised. With no clear policy demand from members, Hill must come back May 12; the silence on what they want speaks to the political pressure school boards in big metros are now under.

title: Carl Wilson Defeats Mamdani's Choice in Council Special Election
why: Carl Wilson swept the District 3 special election with 43% to Lindsey Boylan's 25% as 93% of ballots were counted — a stinging defeat for Mayor Mamdani's choice and the direct payoff of yesterday's New York Focus piece on the Cuomo-aligned super-PAC ad blitz that cratered Boylan's bid. First post-election test of Mamdani's coattails outside the mayoral seat, watched closely by every blue-state progressive coalition trying to convert presidential-year wins into down-ballot infrastructure.

title: Colorado legislature sends $48.6B state budget to governor's desk after final round of tweaks
why: Lawmakers shipped the FY27 budget to Gov. Polis Tuesday after closing a roughly $1.5 billion shortfall — Medicaid took the brunt of the cuts, though a teacher-pipeline dual-enrollment program was rescued for one more year. Sets the template for how blue-state budgets are absorbing the same federal Medicaid pressures hitting Connecticut, Vermont, and California this same week.

title: Lamont moves quickly to tout new CT budget deal
why: Tentative state budget deal includes $270 million in new municipal aid, with Lamont and Lt. Gov. Bysiewicz vowing every town can use the money for property-tax relief — even municipalities that have already adopted local budgets. An unusual mid-cycle override of municipal autonomy that other governors are watching as a potential model for delivering visible relief without reopening local fights.

title: Camp Mystic apologizes to parents of flood victims
why: Edward Eastland's mea culpa to legislators on day two of the flood-investigating committee hearings — that the Eastland family failed to protect 25 campers and two counselors who died in the July 2025 flood — lands as the Texas Rangers, the state licensing agency, and multiple plaintiffs sharpen separate investigations. The watershed moment in a national private-camp-regulation fight that other states are now openly preparing legislation around.

title: New Wisconsin Watch tool makes statewide layoffs easier to track
why: Searchable dashboard of WARN-Act layoff filings going back to 2018, filterable by employer, industry, county, and year — released alongside Wisconsin Watch's earlier immigration-court tracker. A reproducible model for state-level labor reporting at a moment when federal economic data series are getting less reliable, and a tool other state-focused outlets can clone.

title: San Jose police overtime hit $72M in 2025, audit shows
why: The City Auditor finds SJPD overtime jumped 53% over five years to $72M in FY24-25, with 124 sworn officers each clocking more than 1,000 OT hours — much of it on administrative paperwork without supervisor approval. Pairs naturally with police-budget accountability fights playing out in Charlotte, Detroit, and Chicago, and gives reform advocates a reproducible methodology.

title: CT lawmakers weigh future of solar incentives; cost is a key factor
why: Connecticut's residential and commercial solar incentive programs sunset at the end of 2027 unless reauthorized this session — and ratepayer-cost concerns are driving the debate as much as climate goals. Outcome will be a bellwether for whether blue-state solar momentum survives the federal IRA rollback now that the math doesn't pencil the same way.

title: In Louisville, Flock camera locations will stay secret
why: Bipartisan Louisville Metro Council vote sides with LMPD's refusal to disclose the locations of the city's 200+ Flock automatic license-plate readers — three days after Colorado Sun and San José Spotlight surfaced parallel transparency fights with the same vendor. Three cities, three council fights, one company: the surveillance-accountability story of the spring is now firmly cross-regional.

title: Talarico leads both Cornyn, Paxton in new poll of Texas' U.S. Senate race
why: A fresh University of Texas / Texas Politics Project survey shows Democrat James Talarico ahead of both Republican incumbents in head-to-head matchups, with independents breaking 51–29 over Cornyn and 53–28 over Paxton. Cook still rates the seat "likely Republican," but the polling — combined with Talarico's record-breaking $27M haul — puts the GOP runoff and a long-shot Senate flip suddenly in play.

title: How the NYPD Slow-Walked and Shot Down Gang Database Reforms
why: Investigative reconstruction of how Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch quietly killed Mamdani-aligned reforms of the NYPD's gang database — the same database Tisch has publicly defended as central to violence reduction. A live test of how much policy ground a progressive mayor can actually claim against an entrenched top cop, with implications for Chicago, LA, and Oakland's parallel post-election fights.

title: New ICE data shows more than 6,300 arrests in NC since Trump took office, nearly double the prior two years
why: Federal arrest figures through March 10 show ICE has detained 6,374 people across North Carolina since January 2025 — nearly twice the count from the prior two years combined. Establishes a state-level baseline other Southern outlets in Texas, Georgia, and Tennessee will use to benchmark enforcement intensity, and lands as Charlotte's City Council debates a sanctuary-policy resurrection.

title: Does incarcerating someone in a Wisconsin prison for a year cost more than annual state technical school tuition?
why: Wisconsin Watch's fact-check confirms the claim: it costs the state $52,881 per year to incarcerate one person, more than 10x the average annual tuition at Wisconsin's technical colleges. Useful empirical leverage for the budget arguments now playing out in nearly every state pushing prison-reform packages this session.

title: As AI license plate readers spread across Colorado, grassroots movements push back
why: A statewide look at how Flock automatic license-plate-reader cameras are proliferating from cul-de-sacs to highways — and the volunteer networks now mapping every camera, suing for records, and pushing local councils to opt out. Pairs directly with yesterday's San José Spotlight scoop on hundreds of out-of-state agencies tapping Palo Alto's Flock feed: the surveillance-accountability story is now firmly cross-regional.

title: Palo Alto license plate data searched by hundreds of out-of-state agencies
why: Public records obtained by the Spotlight contradict months of public assurances from Palo Alto leaders: hundreds of out-of-state and federal law-enforcement agencies have been searching the city's Flock automatic-license-plate-reader feed via the company's "nationwide lookup" feature since late 2023. A direct surveillance-accountability story that lands in every city that runs Flock cameras.

title: Cuomo Allies Pour Money Into Race Against Lindsey Boylan
why: On the eve of the April 28 special election for City Council District 3, NYF documents a six-figure independent-expenditure surge against Boylan — the former Cuomo aide who first publicly accused him of sexual harassment. The super PAC is funneling spend through a pass-through entity that masks donor names on mailers, a workaround other state IE committees are watching.

title: NC lawmakers unite across aisle to advance Medicaid funding
why: The North Carolina House and Senate near-unanimously moved House Bill 696, drawing $319 million from the state Medicaid Contingency Reserve to keep the program solvent through June. WFAE traces the cost spike to the federal "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," GLP-1 drug uptake and rising autism-treatment demand — pressures that will hit every Medicaid-expansion state in the next budget cycle.

title: Box Elder County delays vote on hyperscale data center, under pressure from protesters and Utah leaders
why: A $4 billion hyperscale data-center plan backed by MIDA and Kevin O'Leary stalled at the Box Elder County Commission after sustained pressure from residents, water districts, and even sitting Utah officials worried about water and power. Joins a growing string of grassroots data-center pushbacks (Port Washington WI, Tucson AZ) reshaping how local governments greenlight AI infrastructure.

title: Camp Mystic counselors lacked training, Texas lawmakers told
why: At today's General Investigating Committee hearing in Austin, an investigator walked lawmakers beat-by-beat through the July 2025 flood that killed 25 campers, two counselors and Camp Mystic's executive director — concluding the camp had no adequate evacuation plan, no flood preparedness supplies, and counselors who had not been trained. With multiple lawsuits pending and the Texas Rangers and state licensing agency both investigating, this is shaping the national debate over private youth-camp regulation.

title: Federal government demands renewal for every healthcare provider that receives Medicaid
why: CMS is requiring every provider that bills Medicaid to re-enroll on a compressed timeline — a paperwork tsunami that small clinics, pediatricians and rural hospitals say will knock dozens off the program. Vermont health regulators warn the same crunch is hitting every state, and dropouts mean longer waits for the country's most vulnerable patients.

title: Texas' new congressional map can be used, Supreme Court rules
why: The U.S. Supreme Court formally overturned a lower-court ruling Monday, clearing Texas' mid-decade map for the 2026 midterms and ending the legal battle that had threatened Republicans' bid to add as many as five new GOP-leaning U.S. House seats. With control of the U.S. House on a knife's edge, this is the single biggest national political development of the day — and a green light for the copycat redistricting fights now underway in Virginia, Missouri and Indiana.

title: Burlington police refused to meet protesters at the table, rejecting a chance for real dialogue
why: After six protesters were arrested trying to stop an ICE abduction on Dorset Street, the state's attorney offered both sides a rare structured mediation. BPD declined — a decision the column documents will surface in suppression motions and reframes the city's already-contentious post-arrest narrative around accountability for police interactions with immigration enforcement.

title: Holiday Club is closing May 17 after 25 years in Uptown
why: The Uptown bar's closure makes way for an apartment building — a small story that maps onto the bigger pattern of legacy small businesses being displaced as Chicago's North Side densifies. Local-character loss as a feature of housing-supply policy is a story other neighborhood outlets in Detroit, Cleveland and Philadelphia are increasingly tracking.

title: Mayor O'Connell's mixed verdict on Tennessee General Assembly session
why: The mayor walked through the legislative session's wins and losses for Nashville: a tourism-tax reallocation he praised, against new state laws asserting control over the airport board and the downtown entertainment district. A textbook case of red-state legislatures preempting blue-city authority — a fight playing out in identical form in Memphis, Atlanta and Houston.

title: 'Billboard Lawyers' Defend Ads and Tactics Amid MTA Push for Lawsuit Reform
why: MTA chair Janno Lieber says personal-injury attorneys "seem to think the MTA is actually spelled ATM," and is pushing Albany for tort reform to rein in payouts. THE CITY's reporting documents the costs and the lawyers' defense — a fight other transit agencies (BART, WMATA, SEPTA) are quietly watching as their own claims budgets balloon.

title: Art Martinez de Vara's influence on Texas local governments
why: An investigative profile of the Paxton-aligned attorney behind the AG's lawsuit accusing Dallas of underfunding its police force — and the broader campaign reshaping how Texas cities fund services. Martinez de Vara's playbook is being copied by GOP attorneys general in Florida, Tennessee and Missouri to put progressive-leaning cities on the defensive.

title: Silicon Valley mental health crisis team at risk of losing funding
why: Santa Clara County's TRUST team — the county's most-used non-police mental health response program — runs out of state seed funding in November, and Gov. Newsom's proposal to make mobile crisis services optional under Medi-Cal would slash reimbursements to roughly 25% of the program's budget. A bellwether for whether California's much-copied non-police-response model is sustainable.

title: Utah wants a new nuclear sector to rise in Brigham City. What will it take to pull it off?
why: Holtec International and Hi Tech Solutions plan a workforce-training center, parts-manufacturing facility, and ten small modular reactors at a Brigham City campus — Utah's biggest bet yet on its post-coal energy economy. Federal SMR licensing is still the bottleneck, but the proposal signals where Western GOP states want to land if the AI-driven power crunch doesn't ease.

title: Sheehy promises White House ballroom bill following D.C. shooting scare
why: Two days after the White House Correspondents' Dinner attack, freshman Sen. Tim Sheehy says he'll introduce legislation authorizing construction of Trump's planned East Wing ballroom — pitched as a security measure. Would be Sheehy's most significant standalone bill in 16 months in office and a marker for how Montana's GOP delegation is positioning ahead of the midterms.

title: Tony Evers revived commutations, but what will Wisconsin's next governor do?
why: Brittany Carloni reports the Democratic governor field broadly plans to keep using clemency, with two candidates breaking from Evers on murder cases — while the GOP front-runner intends to curtail it. A concrete state-level test of whether clemency revival outlives the term-limited governor who started it, with implications for parallel revivals in other Democratic-led states.

title: Meet 2 of the 1 million independent Pa. voters shut out of next month's primary
why: Pennsylvania is one of just eight fully closed-primary states, and Spotlight PA reports its independent rolls have now passed 1 million — voters who can't participate in the May 19 primary. The piece profiles a 74-year-old retired graphic artist and a 22-year-old college student, putting human faces on a fight for open primaries that other closed-primary states are tracking.
